<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<article class="ltx_document ltx_authors_1line">
<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: 
<br class="ltx_break">Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration
</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">
<span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Mooho Song
</span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>Seoul National University
</span></span></span></span>
<span class="ltx_author_before">  </span><span class="ltx_creator ltx_role_author">
<span class="ltx_personname">Jay-Yoon Lee
</span><span id="id1" class="ltx_note ltx_note_frontmatter ltx_thanks_correspondence ltx_role_thanks"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">†</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">thanks: </span>Correspondence author</span></span></span><span class="ltx_author_notes"><span class="ltx_author_notes_content">
<span class="ltx_contact ltx_role_affiliation"><span class="ltx_contact_name">Affiliation: </span>{anmh9161, lee.jayyoon}@snu.ac.kr
</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Multi-hop question answering and retrieval-augmented reasoning require selecting evidence passages that are jointly useful for answering a query.
However, most retrievers still score passages independently or make locally supervised sequential decisions, which can fail when evidence usefulness depends on compatibility among passages.
LLM-based set selection can model such interactions, but its computational cost limits practical use.
We address this gap by formulating multi-hop retrieval as query–set compatibility scoring and propose a set-level retrieval framework.
Our training objective teaches retrievers to rank complete and compatible evidence sets above incomplete, noisy alternatives, making set scoring more robust to variable-length and partially noisy contexts.
We instantiate the framework with two complementary set scorers: <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>, a lightweight late-interaction scorer that applies self-attention over precomputed bi-encoder embeddings for fast candidate-set exploration, and <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>, a cross-encoder-based reranker trained with the same set-level objective.
Experiments on various multi-hop QA benchmarks show that set-level compatibility learning improves retrieval performance and downstream QA task performance.
We further show that the proposed set-level retrievers not only outperform document-level retrievers, but also exhibit complementary retrieval characteristics: combining their outputs yields stronger performance than simply retrieving more passages from a single document-level retriever.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;"></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Document retrieval has traditionally focused on selecting the single most relevant passage for a given query.
However, many reasoning-intensive tasks such as multi-hop QA require retrieving a <em id="S1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">set of evidence passages</em>, where the usefulness of each passage is inherently dependent on the others.
In such settings, retrieving individual passages in independent manner is insufficient: a passage that is useful in isolation may become uninformative or even misleading when combined with an incompatible context.
This interdependence makes multi-hop retrieval fundamentally a <em id="S1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">set-level</em> problem, rendering standard single-passage retrieval approaches inadequate.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recent work such as <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al. (2025)</a></cite> explicitly highlights this limitation and proposes retrieving sets of passages rather than individual passages.
However, their approach relies on LLM-based set selection, resulting in substantial computational and memory overhead that limits its practicality in large-scale or latency-sensitive settings.
Similarly, although <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite> does not explicitly discuss the limitations of single-passage retrieval, it also aims to retrieve multiple objects jointly by leveraging structured relationships across heterogeneous sources.
However, its retrieval pipeline depends on both an LLM and an MIP solver, incurring high computational cost.
These approaches suggest the importance of set-level reasoning, but also highlight a central challenge: making set-level retrieval computationally practical.
A useful set-level retrieval model should be able to account for global compatibility among passages while remaining efficient enough to search over many candidate passage sets.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2607.05712v1/side_by_side_paper_figure2.svg" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/150;" width="452" height="150"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
Summary of our main empirical findings.
Methods involving <span id="S1.F1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> or <span id="S1.F1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> are our set-level retrieval methods.
(a) Set-level methods improve QA performance in several settings, and combining <span id="S1.F1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S1.F1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> with document-level CE yields the strongest results.
(b) Macro-average QA EM using Qwen3 as the first-stage retriever, decomposed by overlap with CE<sub id="S1.F1.13" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>.
Compared with CE<sub id="S1.F1.14" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S1.F1.14.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">10</span></sub>, <math id="S1.F1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ParaSet</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">SetCE</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math> recovers more CE<sub id="S1.F1.15" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>-missed examples and achieves higher overall EM, indicating complementary evidence recovery.
See § <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 End-to-End Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> and § <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Complementarity of Document-Level and Set-Level Scoring ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Non-LLM sequential retrieval methods provide a more computationally efficient alternative.
For example, although <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a></cite> does not explicitly frame its motivation around set retrieval, its cross-encoder scorer can be directly used for multi-hop QA by iteratively constructing a retrieval chain using beam search.
This procedure enables conditioning on previously retrieved evidence without relying on LLM-based passage selection.
However, the training signal remains <em id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">local</em>: the pointwise binary classification (BCE) objective supervises whether each candidate is a correct ‘next passage’ given the current prefix, rather than directly optimizing the global compatibility between the query and the <em id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">entire</em> evidence set.
In addition, such models are typically trained under a fixed-hop regime with limited prefix lengths, whereas inference can expose them to longer and partially corrupted prefixes due to error accumulation.
As a result, the scoring function is not explicitly encouraged to robustly evaluate query–set interactions under variable-length or noisy retrieval chains. We provide a controlled analysis of this failure mode in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Robustness Analysis of Sequential Set Scoring ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>, where sequential scorers trained with local supervision show substantial degradation under longer and noisier prefixes, while the same architecture fine-tuned with our set-level objective remains more robust.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> previews our main empirical findings:
set-level methods improve QA performance in several settings, and CE-augmented set-level retrieval yields further gains by recovering examples missed by CE<sub id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>.
We discuss these results in § <a href="#S4.SS2" title="4.2 End-to-End Performance ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.2</span></a> and § <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Complementarity of Document-Level and Set-Level Scoring ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Our Approach.</h4>

<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Motivated by these limitations, we reframe multi-hop retrieval as a <em id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">query–set scoring</em> problem: instead of ranking passages independently or making local next-passage decisions, our approach directly scores the compatibility between a query and a candidate passage set.
This formulation separates two challenges: learning a compatibility-aware set scorer and searching the combinatorial space of passage sets efficiently.
Our contributions are summarized as follows:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize ltx_leftmargin_flush">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Query–set scoring for multi-hop retrieval.</span>
We formulate multi-hop retrieval as directly scoring the compatibility between a query and a candidate passage set.
Unlike independent passage rerankers or conditional next-passage scorers, which decompose evidence selection into local decisions, our framework learns a direct query–set scoring function.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first non-LLM neural framework that
trains retrieval models to explicitly score query–set compatibility.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Set-level compatibility learning.</span>
We introduce a model-agnostic margin-based objective that ranks compatible evidence sets above incomplete, noisy, or corrupt alternatives.
We show that the proposed objective can effectively train models across different architectures, including lightweight set scorers and cross-encoder-based set rerankers, improving their robustness under variable-length and noisy retrieval contexts.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Efficient set-level retrieve-and-rerank.</span>
To avoid exhaustive scoring over <math id="S1.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{N}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{N}-1</annotation></semantics></math> possible non-empty subsets, we use beam search to approximate high-scoring passage sets.
We further instantiate this search procedure with two complementary set scorers analogous to bi-encoders and cross-encoders in standard retrieval: <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> efficiently explores candidate sets over precomputed embeddings, while <span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> performs fine-grained set-level reranking with the same compatibility objective.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Complementarity with passage-level retrieval.</span>
We show that passage-level and set-level scoring capture different evidence signals: passage-level cross-encoders identify individually salient passages, whereas set-level scoring captures globally compatible combinations.
Combining the two yields further gains, showing that set-level retrieval is a complementary component rather than a replacement for passage-level scoring.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Multi-Passage Retrieval for Multi-hop QA</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Early retrieval-based approaches to multi-hop QA retrieve multiple passages independently, typically by selecting the top-<math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> passages for a query using dense retrievers or cross-encoders <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Karpukhin et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Izacard and Grave, 2021</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lewis et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Min et al., 2019</a>)</cite>.
Although such methods can aggregate information from multiple sources, they assume independent passage relevance and do not explicitly model interactions among retrieved evidence.
This limits their ability to select passages whose usefulness depends on compatibility with other passages.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Sequential Multi-hop Retrieval</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To move beyond independent retrieval, iterative methods repeatedly retrieve passages conditioned on an evolving query or reasoning state <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xiong et al., 2020</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Press et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yue et al., 2024</a>)</cite>.
Similarly, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a></cite> propose a cross-encoder retriever that predicts the next passage conditioned on the query and previously retrieved passages, enabling non-LLM sequential multi-hop retrieval.
These methods can condition on intermediate context, but they still formulate retrieval as a sequence of local decisions rather than directly scoring the compatibility of the retrieved set as a whole.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Set-level Retrieval</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A more direct approach is to retrieve evidence through global set selection.
For example, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al. (2025)</a></cite> formulate retrieval as a set selection problem and use LLMs to jointly reason over candidate passages.
Relatedly, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al. (2025)</a></cite> consider structured multi-object retrieval, where relationships among retrieved items are explicitly modeled during inference.
Although these approaches capture interactions among retrieved items, their reliance on LLM-based reasoning or complex inference pipelines incurs substantial computational and memory overhead.
In contrast, our approach directly scores a large number of candidate passage sets in a parallel manner with lightweight neural scorers, enabling efficient and scalable set-level retrieval without LLM-based selection.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F2.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><img src="2607.05712v1/paraset_setce_figure.png" id="S2.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/121;" width="476" height="121" alt="Refer to caption">
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S2.F2.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2607.05712v1/hotpot_contriever_max_recall.svg" id="S2.F2.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/383;" width="476" height="383"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>
Overview and empirical behavior of our set-level retrieval framework.
(a) Comparison of document-level and set-level scoring architectures.
Bi-encoder and cross-encoder models score query–passage pairs independently, whereas ParaSet and SetCE score query–set compatibility.
ParaSet performs lightweight late interaction over precomputed and KV-cached embeddings for efficient candidate-set exploration, while SetCE jointly encodes the query and candidate tokens as an expressive set-level reranker.
(b) Retrieved-set quality of <span id="S2.F2.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> on HotpotQA.
Here, <math id="S2.F2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> is the first-stage candidate-passage budget and <math id="S2.F2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of top candidate sets proposed by <span id="S2.F2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>.
Max Recall improves as <math id="S2.F2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.F2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> increase, even though the set search space grows exponentially with <math id="S2.F2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{K}</annotation></semantics></math>.
For example, <math id="S2.F2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B_{K}=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B_{K}=50</annotation></semantics></math> induces <math id="S2.F2.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{50}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mn>2</mn><mn>50</mn></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{50}</annotation></semantics></math> possible subsets.
See Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Candidate Quality and Standalone Performance of ParaSet ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a> for analysis on other datasets.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Set-Level Query–Set Scoring</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We propose a set-level retrieval framework that directly scores the compatibility between a query and a candidate passage set.
The framework has two components: a model-agnostic set-level compatibility learning objective, and efficient set scorers for exploring and reranking candidate passage sets.
We instantiate it with two complementary models.
<span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> is a lightweight attention-based scorer over bi-encoder embeddings that efficiently explores promising sets, while <span id="S3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> is a more expressive cross-encoder-based scorer trained with the same objective for fine-grained reranking.
Together, they form a set-level retrieve-and-rerank pipeline analogous to standard document retrieval: <span id="S3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> serves as a fast set-level explorer, and <span id="S3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> as an expressive set-level reranker.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Set-level Compatibility Learning</h3>

<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce a compatibility learning objective that trains a scorer to rank passage sets by their usefulness as a whole.
Let the gold evidence set for query <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> be</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{q}=\{d_{1}^{+},\dots,d_{k}^{+}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{q}=\{d_{1}^{+},\dots,d_{k}^{+}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Given a scoring function <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S(q,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S(q,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math>, we aim to assign higher scores to sets that are more compatible with the query and the gold evidence structure, and lower scores to incomplete, noisy, or incompatible alternatives.
The objective is model-agnostic and can train both lightweight set scorers such as <span id="S3.SS1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> and cross-encoder-based scorers such as <span id="S3.SS1.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Candidate set construction.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct candidate sets with varying degrees of compatibility.
First, we generate structured perturbations of the gold set using addition, elimination, and interchange:</p>
<table id="S3.EGx1" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.Ex2"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><span id="S3.Ex2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">Addition:</span></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle N=\mathcal{G}_{q}\cup\{d^{-}\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle N=\mathcal{G}_{q}\cup\{d^{-}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex3"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><span id="S3.Ex3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">Elimination:</span></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle N\subset\mathcal{G}_{q},\quad N\neq\varnothing," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>⊂</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle N\subset\mathcal{G}_{q},\quad N\neq\varnothing,</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="S3.Ex4"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><span id="S3.Ex4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_markedasmath ltx_font_bold">Interchange:</span></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.Ex4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle N=(\mathcal{G}_{q}\cup\{d^{-}\})\setminus\{d_{i}^{+}\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>∪</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∖</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>i</mi><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle N=(\mathcal{G}_{q}\cup\{d^{-}\})\setminus\{d_{i}^{+}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="d^{-}\notin\mathcal{G}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo>∉</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">d^{-}\notin\mathcal{G}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>.
These perturbations expose the model to over-complete, under-complete, and corrupted evidence sets.
Second, we add in-batch negatives by using gold evidence sets from other queries and randomly sampled subsets of passages appearing in the mini-batch.
These negatives can be plausible at the passage level but incompatible with the current query as a set.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Set quality ordering.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Rather than assigning absolute scores, we impose a relative ordering over candidate sets.
In our experiments, set quality is defined by agreement with the gold evidence set and ranked lexicographically by prioritizing recall first and precision second.
This reflects the needs of multi-hop QA, where covering required evidence is essential while avoiding unnecessary distractors remains useful.
A concrete example of this ordering, including addition, elimination, and interchange perturbations, is provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS3" title="A.3 Example of Set Quality Ordering ‣ Appendix A Details of the ParaSet and Beam-Search Inference ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H\succ L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>≻</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H\succ L</annotation></semantics></math> denote that <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> is more compatible than <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> under this ordering.
For each ordered pair <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(H,L)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(H,L)</annotation></semantics></math>, we use the margin-based ranking loss</p>
<table id="S3.Ex5" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\ell(H,L)=\max\left(0,\;\gamma-S(q,H)+S(q,L)\right)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>max</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo>(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>γ</mi><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ell(H,L)=\max\left(0,\;\gamma-S(q,H)+S(q,L)\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\gamma" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>γ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\gamma</annotation></semantics></math> is a margin hyperparameter.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Training objective.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each query, we construct a candidate pool <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{C}</annotation></semantics></math> containing the gold set, structured perturbations, and in-batch negatives.
We first require the gold set to outrank all other candidates:
<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{pos-all}}^{q}=\sum_{L\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\{\mathcal{G}_{q}\}}\ell(\mathcal{G}_{q},L)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>pos-all</mtext><mi>q</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒞</mi><mo>∖</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{pos-all}}^{q}=\sum_{L\in\mathcal{C}\setminus\{\mathcal{G}_{q}\}}\ell(\mathcal{G}_{q},L).</annotation></semantics></math>
We further impose fine-grained constraints between adjacent compatibility levels:
<math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{adj}}^{q}=\sum_{(H,L)\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{adj}}}\ell(H,L)," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>adj</mtext><mi>q</mi></msubsup><mo rspace="0.111em">=</mo><mrow><msub><mo>∑</mo><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>adj</mtext></msub></mrow></msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">ℓ</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{adj}}^{q}=\sum_{(H,L)\in\mathcal{P}_{\text{adj}}}\ell(H,L),</annotation></semantics></math>
where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{P}_{\text{adj}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒫</mi><mtext>adj</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{P}_{\text{adj}}</annotation></semantics></math> contains ordered pairs in which <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> is ranked immediately above <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math>.
The final objective is</p>
<table id="S3.EGx2" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_align ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="S3.E1"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="S3.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{final}}=\underset{q}{\sum}(\mathcal{L}_{\text{pos-all}}^{q}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{adj}}^{q})," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>final</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mstyle displaystyle="true"><mo movablelimits="false">∑</mo></mstyle><mo mathsize="0.700em">𝑞</mo></munder><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>pos-all</mtext><mi>q</mi></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msubsup><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>adj</mtext><mi>q</mi></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\text{final}}=\underset{q}{\sum}(\mathcal{L}_{\text{pos-all}}^{q}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{adj}}^{q}),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> controls the weight of adjacent-ranking constraints.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Applying this objective to a sequential cross-encoder yields <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>, which preserves the original architecture and inference procedure but replaces local next-passage supervision with set-level compatibility learning.
Applying it to a lightweight embedding-based scorer yields <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>, enabling efficient exploration of the passage-set space.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Lightweight Set Exploration with ParaSet</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Set-level scoring requires efficient search, since a pool of <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> passages induces <math id="S3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{n}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{n}-1</annotation></semantics></math> non-empty subsets.
We introduce <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> (Parallel Set-Scorer), a lightweight scorer designed to explore this combinatorial space.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Architecture.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> operates on bi-encoder representations.
Given a query embedding <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math> and passage embeddings <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math>, it scores a candidate set by forming a short sequence consisting of a learnable <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[CLS]</span> token, the query embedding, and the embeddings of passages in the set.
A single multi-head self-attention layer performs late interaction over this sequence, and the final score is computed from the resulting <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[CLS]</span> representation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The computation required for <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> is substantially smaller than cross-encoder set scoring because it avoids joint encoding of raw query–passage text.
Moreover, since passage embeddings are query-independent and <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> uses only a shallow attention layer, the passage-side key and value projections can be precomputed and cached.
At inference time, scoring a candidate set therefore starts from cached passage-side representations and only requires lightweight query-dependent computation and dot-product attention over the selected elements.
This enables many candidate sets for the same query to be scored efficiently in parallel.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Thus, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> serves as a set-level retriever analogue of a bi-encoder: its role is to propose and prioritize promising passage sets that can be passed to a stronger reranker such as <span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Beam-search set retrieval.</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given a candidate pool, we approximate</p>
<table id="S3.Ex6" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{\star}=\underset{S\subseteq[n],\,S\neq\varnothing}{\arg\max}\;s_{\theta}(q,S)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>max</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">S</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">⊆</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">[</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em">n</mi><mo maxsize="0.700em" minsize="0.700em">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo mathsize="0.700em" rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">S</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">≠</mo><mi mathsize="0.700em" mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{\star}=\underset{S\subseteq[n],\,S\neq\varnothing}{\arg\max}\;s_{\theta}(q,S),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">using beam search with batched set scoring.
The beam is initialized with the top-<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> singleton sets, and we maintain an accumulated candidate pool <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{acc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>acc</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{acc}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
At each step <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math>, each beam subset of size <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t-1</annotation></semantics></math> is expanded by adding one new passage.
The generated size-<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> subsets are deduplicated and scored in parallel with ParaSet.
The top-<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> size-<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>t</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t</annotation></semantics></math> subsets are retained as the next beam, while all scored candidates are added to the accumulated pool <math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{acc}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒮</mi><mi>acc</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{acc}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Unlike standard beam search, we do not return only the final beam.
Instead, we select the highest-scoring subset among all accumulated candidates:
<math id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\hat{S}=\underset{S\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{acc}}}{\arg\max}\;s_{\theta}(q,S)." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>S</mi><mo>^</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mrow><munder accentunder="true"><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>max</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathsize="0.700em">S</mi><mo mathsize="0.700em">∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic" mathsize="0.700em">𝒮</mi><mi mathsize="0.710em">acc</mi></msub></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>θ</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\hat{S}=\underset{S\in\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{acc}}}{\arg\max}\;s_{\theta}(q,S).</annotation></semantics></math>
Additional details are provided in Appendix <a href="#A1.SS4" title="A.4 Beam-Search Set Retrieval ‣ Appendix A Details of the ParaSet and Beam-Search Inference ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A.4</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Expressive Set Reranking with SetCE</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> enables efficient exploration, a shallow embedding-based model may not provide the most expressive compatibility estimate.
We therefore instantiate <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>, a cross-encoder-based set scorer trained with the same objective in Eq. <a href="#S3.E1" title="In Training objective. ‣ 3.1 Set-level Compatibility Learning ‣ 3 Set-Level Query–Set Scoring ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> is obtained by fine-tuning a cross-encoder architecture that simply processes all tokens from a query and documents together. We essentially keep its architecture and inference procedure the same as our baseline sequential retriever (ListCE) to
disentangle the effect of our proposed set-level compatibility learning from architectural changes.
Unlike pointwise next-passage supervision of ListCE, <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> is explicitly optimized to evaluate the compatibility of an entire passage set with the query.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In the full pipeline, <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> first explores the combinatorial set space and suggests a small number of candidate sets.
<span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> then reranks these proposed sets with more expressive set-level scoring.
This mirrors the standard retrieve-and-rerank paradigm, but operates over passage sets rather than individual passages.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>
Example-level complementarity with document-level CE.
Panel (a) reports overlap with CE<sub id="S4.T2.4" class="ltx_sub">5</sub> macro-averaged over all six dataset/retriever settings, where values are normalized by <math id="S4.T2.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\cup\mathrm{CE}_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\cup\mathrm{CE}_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>.
The last column reports the macro-average EM of the CE-augmented variant <math id="S4.T2.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Panel (b) reports question-type enrichment ratios for <math id="S4.T2.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M=\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ParaSet</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">SetCE</mtext></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M=\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE}</annotation></semantics></math>, averaged over the two first-stage retrievers.
Ratios are computed as the fraction of each question type in <math id="S4.T2.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\setminus\mathrm{CE}_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∖</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\setminus\mathrm{CE}_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> divided by its fraction in <math id="S4.T2.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{CE}_{5}\setminus M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>∖</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{CE}_{5}\setminus M</annotation></semantics></math>.
Ratios above 1 indicate question types more concentrated in the set-level-only region, while ratios below 1 indicate types more concentrated in the CE<sub id="S4.T2.5" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>-only region.
</figcaption>
<div id="S4.T2.6" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:114.2pt;vertical-align:-54.8pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-13.5pt,4.5pt) scale(0.927275201407265,0.927275201407265) ;">

<tr id="S4.T2.6.1.2" class="ltx_tr">

</span></div>
</figure>
<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate our framework across multi-hop QA benchmarks, first-stage retrievers, and retrieval settings.
Our experiments focus on three questions:
(1) Can set-level retrieval improve downstream QA performance?
(2) Beyond aggregate performance, does set-level retrieval recover evidence missed by document-level retrieval?
(3) Can retrieve-and-rerank in set search achieve a favorable trade-off between retrieval quality and computational cost?</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Benchmarks.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate on three multi-hop question answering benchmarks: HotpotQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, 2WikiMultihopQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and MuSiQue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
HotpotQA consists of 2-hop questions, while 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue include questions requiring up to 4 hops.
These datasets allow us to assess retrieval and downstream QA performance across different reasoning depths and evidence structures.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">First-stage retrievers.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use dense bi-encoder retrievers to construct the initial candidate pool for all reranking and set-level search methods.
We evaluate both Contriever <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Izacard et al., 2022</a>)</cite> and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to examine whether set-level scoring remains effective under different first-stage retrieval quality.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Compared methods.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare methods representing different retrieval paradigms.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bi</span> directly uses the top passages from the first-stage retriever.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CE</span> is a passage-level cross-encoder reranker based on <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ms-marco-electra-base</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hugging Face, 2021</a>)</cite>, which scores query–passage pairs independently.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ListCE</span> is a sequential cross-encoder scorer based on <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a></cite>, implemented with a <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">deberta-v3-base</span> backbone and trained with pointwise next-passage classification.
It expands retrieval chains with beam search and selects the highest-scoring evaluated passage set.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">SetCE</span> uses the same architecture and inference procedure as ListCE, but is fine-tuned with our set-level compatibility objective, isolating the effect of set-level supervision.
<span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ParaSet+SetCE</span> is our set-level retrieve-and-rerank pipeline: <span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> first explores the combinatorial passage-set space and proposes candidate sets, and SetCE reranks them with one forward pass per set.
This avoids applying SetCE throughout beam search while retaining expressive set-level reranking.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">CE augmentation notation.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">CE<sub id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">k</span></sub> denotes the document-level CE’s QA performance when the top-<math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> CE-ranked passages are provided to the reader LLM.
We use CE<sub id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub">5</sub> to denote default document-level CE retriever results, and CE<sub id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">10</span></sub> denotes outcome of expanded retrieval.
For a set-level method <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, we denote its CE-augmented variant by <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math>, where the final context for the reader is formed by combining <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>’s best-ranked set-level output with the top-5 passages selected by CE.
This notation distinguishes retrieval augmentation, <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math>, from example-level set operations such as <math id="S4.SS1.SSS0.Px4.p1.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\cup\mathrm{CE}_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\cup\mathrm{CE}_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> used in the overlap analysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>End-to-End Performance</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports macro-average downstream QA performance across available hop categories; hop-wise results are provided in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Hop-wise End-to-End QA Performance ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.
For each method, the selected passages are given with fixed few-shot exemplars to a frozen LLM (<span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">gpt-4o-mini</span>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citeauthor"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI</a></cite>) for answer generation, so performance differences reflect the upstream retrieval stage.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate all methods with Contriever and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B as first-stage retrievers.
Bi and CE<sub id="S4.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_sub">5</sub> provide five passages to the reader.
<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">CE</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ListCE</span>, and <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> rerank a fixed pool of 20 passages, while <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> search over up to 50 passages due to the lower cost of lightweight set exploration.
For <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>, <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> first proposes candidate passage sets and <span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> reranks them with one forward pass per set.
We also report CE<sub id="S4.SS2.p2.1.12" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S4.SS2.p2.1.12.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">10</span></sub> and <math id="S4.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ParaSet</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">SetCE</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math> to evaluate whether combining document-level and set-level evidence improves performance beyond simply returning more CE-ranked passages.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Several trends are worth noting.
First, set-level compatibility learning improves over locally supervised sequential retrieval.
Since <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ListCE</span> and <span id="S4.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> share the same architecture and inference procedure, their comparison isolates the effect of replacing pointwise next-passage supervision with our set-level compatibility objective.
This is consistent with Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Robustness Analysis of Sequential Set Scoring ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>, where local supervision becomes brittle under longer or noisier prefixes, while set-level learning remains more stable.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Second, <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> shows that set-level retrieval can be practical.
Instead of applying a cross-encoder throughout beam search, <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> explores candidate sets efficiently and <span id="S4.SS2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> reranks only the resulting pool.
This retrieve-and-rerank design achieves competitive performance, supporting the division of labor between lightweight set exploration and expressive set reranking.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, the strong performance of <math id="S4.SS2.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ParaSet</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">SetCE</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math> suggests that document-level and set-level retrieval provide complementary evidence, which we analyze next.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Complementarity of Document-Level and Set-Level Scoring</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S1.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>(b) suggests that the gain from CE-augmented set-level retrieval is not simply due to preserving examples already solved by CE<sub id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>.
Compared with CE<sub id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">10</span></sub>, <math id="S4.SS3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ParaSet</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">SetCE</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math> loses a similar amount of CE<sub id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>-correct examples, but recovers a larger number of CE<sub id="S4.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>-missed examples.
We therefore analyze this complementarity more systematically at the example level.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Where Set-Level Retrieval Differs from CE.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For a retrieval method <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, we partition examples solved by either <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math> or CE<sub id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub">5</sub> into <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\setminus\mathrm{CE}_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∖</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\setminus\mathrm{CE}_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{CE}_{5}\setminus M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>∖</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{CE}_{5}\setminus M</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\cap\mathrm{CE}_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\cap\mathrm{CE}_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(a) reports this partition, macro-averaged over all six dataset/retriever settings and normalized by <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\cup\mathrm{CE}_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∪</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\cup\mathrm{CE}_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results show that <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> has the largest <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\setminus\mathrm{CE}_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∖</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\setminus\mathrm{CE}_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> region and the smallest <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M\cap\mathrm{CE}_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M\cap\mathrm{CE}_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> region among the compared set-level methods.
This indicates that <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> overlaps less with CE<sub id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_sub">5</sub> and recovers more CE<sub id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.6" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>-missed examples, suggesting stronger complementarity than <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ListCE</span> or <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>.
Importantly, this occurs despite its lower inference cost: <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> performs lightweight set exploration, and <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> reranks only a reduced candidate-set pool.
The augmented EM column further shows that this complementarity translates into the strongest CE-augmented QA performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Question-type asymmetry.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next ask where this complementarity comes from.
For 2-hop questions, we distinguish <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">parallel</em> questions, where supporting passages can often be identified independently, from <em id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">sequential</em> questions, where evidence must be composed as a chain.
Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>(b) shows that sequential questions are more concentrated in the set-level-only region, whereas parallel questions are more concentrated in the CE<sub id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_sub">5</sub>-only region.
This suggests that set-level retrieval complements CE particularly when evidence passages must be selected through sequential composition, while CE remains strong when passages can be retrieved independently through passage-level relevance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Combining CE with set-level methods.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we evaluate whether this complementarity is robust across answer-generation LLMs.
Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Combining CE with set-level methods. ‣ 4.3 Complementarity of Document-Level and Set-Level Scoring ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports QA EM for CE<sub id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">10</span></sub>, SetCE<math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">ParaSet</mtext><mo>+</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">SetCE</mtext></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(\texttt{ParaSet}{}+\texttt{SetCE})_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math> across multiple reader LLMs and first-stage retrievers.
Across GPT-4o-mini, GPT-5.4-nano<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI (2026)</a></cite>, and Gemini-2.5-flash-lite<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Google (2026)</a></cite>, combining CE<sub id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_sub">5</sub> with <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> generally yields the strongest performance.
Thus, the benefit of CE augmentation is not tied to a particular reader model, but reflects complementary evidence recovered during retrieval.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T3" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>
Downstream QA EM (%) with CE augmentation across answer-generation LLMs.
For each model <math id="S4.T3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>M</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M</annotation></semantics></math>, the CE-augmented variant <math id="S4.T3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="M_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">M_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math> combines the method’s top-ranked set with CE<sub id="S4.T3.4" class="ltx_sub">5</sub> passages.
For CE, augmentation corresponds to CE<sub id="S4.T3.5" class="ltx_sub"><span id="S4.T3.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">10</span></sub>, i.e., expanding the returned passages from top-5 to 10.
</figcaption>
