</span></div>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Trade-off</h3>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2607.05712v1/contriever_tradeoff_hotpot_f5.svg" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/226;" width="429" height="226"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>
Retrieval <math id="S4.F3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> versus latency on HotpotQA using Contriever as the first-stage retriever.
Each curve varies the number of first-stage candidate passages with <math id="S4.F3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\in\{5,10,\dots,50\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\in\{5,10,\dots,50\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and each point corresponds to one value of <math id="S4.F3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>.
The <math id="S4.F3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-axis reports per-query latency on a logarithmic scale; for all methods except Bi, we exclude the first-stage bi-encoder retrieval time.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We next evaluate retrieval quality and computational efficiency.
Because standard retrieval F1 does not align well with downstream QA performance, we first identify a retrieval-side metric that better reflects answerability.
In multi-hop QA, missing a required evidence passage can be more harmful than including extra passages, since the reader may ignore some distractors but cannot recover absent evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To examine this, we compute retrieval precision, recall, and
<math id="S4.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>β</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            <math id="footnote1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\beta}=\frac{(1+\beta^{2})\cdot\mathrm{Precision}\cdot\mathrm{Recall}}{\beta^{2}\cdot\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>β</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>Precision</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>Recall</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>Precision</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>Recall</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\beta}=\frac{(1+\beta^{2})\cdot\mathrm{Precision}\cdot\mathrm{Recall}}{\beta^{2}\cdot\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}.</annotation></semantics></math>
</span></span></span>
scores across all methods, datasets, and first-stage retrievers used in our end-to-end QA experiments, and measure their Pearson correlation with QA EM.
As shown in Table <a href="#A3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ C.1 Correlation between Retrieval Metrics and QA EM ‣ Appendix C Additional Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Results ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, precision alone correlates weakly with QA EM, while recall is substantially more predictive.
The correlation peaks at <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> and slightly decreases for larger <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>, suggesting that downstream QA is strongly coverage-sensitive but still benefits from penalizing overly noisy contexts.
We therefore use <math id="S4.SS4.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> as the primary retrieval metric in our effectiveness–efficiency analysis.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Trade-off ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> reports the HotpotQA trade-off between retrieval <math id="S4.SS4.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> and per-query latency as the first-stage candidate pool size varies.
We show HotpotQA in the main text and provide the corresponding results for other datasets in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Additional Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Results ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Several observations can be drawn from Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Trade-off ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.
First, cross-encoder-based set retrieval can improve retrieval quality, but incurs high latency because the scorer is repeatedly invoked during beam search over candidate sets.
Second, <span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> provides a lightweight alternative for exploring this set space.
Third, <span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> offers a practical compromise: <span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> performs the combinatorial exploration, and <span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> reranks only the reduced candidate-set pool.
This reduces per-query latency from 0.555s for beam-search <span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> at <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=20</annotation></semantics></math> to 0.116s for <span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> at <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=50</annotation></semantics></math>, while still using a larger first-stage candidate pool.
Thus, our pipeline improves the effectiveness–efficiency trade-off by avoiding expensive cross-encoder scoring over the full beam-search space.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Comparison with LLM-based and Agentic Retrieval</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further compare our framework with two stronger retrieval paradigms: LLM-based set selection and multi-step agentic retrieval.
First, we compare with an LLM-based set selector inspired by SETR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, which jointly selects evidence using an LLM.
As shown in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Comparison with LLM-based Set Retrieval ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>, <span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> achieves competitive performance while being about <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="17.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>17.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">17.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than the LLM-based selector.
With CE augmentation, our method further outperforms the LLM-based selector, yet still remains about <math id="S4.SS5.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="10.7\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10.7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10.7\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster.
This suggests that much of the benefit of set-level evidence selection can be obtained without expensive LLM-based set selection.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Second, we compare with IRCoT-style agentic retrieval <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, which interleaves LLM-driven query generation, retrieval, and reasoning over multiple steps.
Unlike such multi-step pipelines, our approach performs retrieval in a single stage by directly scoring candidate evidence sets.
As shown in Table <a href="#A5.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ E.3 Comparison with Agentic Retrieval Pipelines ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, our single-step set-level methods achieve competitive or stronger performance while avoiding repeated LLM calls and iterative retrieval.
Moreover, <span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE<math id="S4.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>CE</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}_{+\mathrm{CE}_{5}}</annotation></semantics></math></span> is about <math id="S4.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="44.1\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>44.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">44.1\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than the multi-step CE pipeline, while achieving stronger downstream performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Additional Analyses</h3>

<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct additional analyses to better understand the behavior and efficiency of set retrieval.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Candidate quality of ParaSet.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As <span id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> is intended as a lightweight candidate-set generator, its top-1 performance alone can underestimate its utility.
In our retrieve-and-rerank pipeline, <span id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> does not merely rerank individual passages.
Instead, it proposes the top-<math id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> candidate evidence sets, and <span id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> selects the best set among them.
Thus, <math id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of candidate sets passed to the reranker, not the number of passages returned to the reader.
We analyze Max-F1@<math id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> over these top-<math id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> candidate sets and find that <span id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> often includes high-quality evidence sets within a small candidate-set pool, supporting its role in retrieve-and-rerank pipelines.
Full results are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS2" title="E.2 Candidate Quality and Standalone Performance of ParaSet ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ablations.</h4>

<div id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We further analyze the beam width used in <span id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> search and the adjacent-ranking weight <math id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In Training objective. ‣ 3.1 Set-level Compatibility Learning ‣ 3 Set-Level Query–Set Scoring ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>).
Increasing beam width from 1 to 2 improves retrieval quality, but larger beams yield diminishing returns while increasing latency.
The effect of <math id="S4.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is dataset-dependent, suggesting that the optimal coverage–parsimony trade-off varies across benchmarks.
Full results are provided in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS4" title="E.4 Beam Width Analysis ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.4</span></a> and Appendix <a href="#A5.SS5" title="E.5 Effect of Adjacent-Ranking Weight ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We studied multi-hop retrieval as a query–set scoring problem, where evidence passages should be selected by joint compatibility rather than independent relevance.
We proposed a set-level retrieval framework that combines compatibility learning with efficient set search, making query–set scoring practical over combinatorial passage sets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Experiments show that set-level compatibility learning is an effective supervision signal for multi-hop QA.
<span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> improves robustness over locally supervised sequential retrieval under the same architecture and inference procedure, while <span id="S5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="S5.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> enables practical retrieve-and-rerank with lightweight set exploration followed by expressive reranking.
Our analyses further show that set-level retrieval complements document-level reranking: combining set-level evidence with CE outputs yields stronger performance than relying on either paradigm alone.
These results suggest that set-level retrieval is a useful direction for efficient retrieval systems that support multi-hop question answering and retrieval-augmented reasoning.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">First, our current framework uses relatively simple search and combination strategies.
For example, CE-augmentation framework combines document-level and set-level outputs through a direct union, and <span id="Sx1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> uses beam search for set exploration.
While these choices are simple and effective, more adaptive strategies could further improve performance, such as dynamically deciding when to rely on document-level versus set-level evidence, learning how to merge retrieved sets, or allocating different candidate budgets depending on query difficulty.
Second, our experiments focus on multi-hop QA benchmarks with relatively short passages and controlled evidence annotations.
Real-world retrieval-augmented reasoning may involve longer documents, noisier corpora, ambiguous evidence boundaries, and larger-scale candidate pools.
Extending set-level compatibility learning to these settings, potentially with indexing or approximate search methods over passage sets, is an important direction for future work.</p>
</div>
</section>

<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_author">S. Min, V. Zhong, L. Zettlemoyer, and H. Hajishirzi</span>

<span class="ltx_bibblock"><span class="ltx_text ltx_bib_title">Multi-hop reading comprehension through question decomposition and rescoring</span>.

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Details of the ParaSet and Beam-Search Inference</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This appendix provides implementation-level details of the <span id="A1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> scorer and its beam-search inference procedure.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.1 </span>Notation</h3>

<div id="A1.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Given an input query, a bi-encoder produces a query embedding (<math id="A1.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>) and candidate passage embeddings <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}</annotation></semantics></math>.
We write a candidate set by its index subset <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S\subseteq[n]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⊆</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S\subseteq[n]</annotation></semantics></math> and denote the corresponding passage embeddings by <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{p_{i}\}_{i\in S}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{p_{i}\}_{i\in S}</annotation></semantics></math>.
In the attention layer, we use (<math id="A1.SS1.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>Q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q</annotation></semantics></math>) for the attention query vector, and (<math id="A1.SS1.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K,V" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>V</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K,V</annotation></semantics></math>) for key/value vectors:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex7" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex7.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Q=W_{Q}q,\qquad K_{i}=W_{K}p_{i},\qquad V_{i}=W_{V}p_{i}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>K</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>V</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Q=W_{Q}q,\qquad K_{i}=W_{K}p_{i},\qquad V_{i}=W_{V}p_{i}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We use a beam width <math id="A1.SS1.p1.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.2 </span>Forward Computation of the Set Score</h3>

<div id="A1.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To score a set <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, we construct an input sequence consisting of a learnable <span id="A1.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[CLS]</span> token, the query embedding (<math id="A1.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>q</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q</annotation></semantics></math>), and the passage embeddings in the set:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex8" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex8.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x(S)=(\texttt{[CLS]},\,q,\,\{p_{i}\}_{i\in S})." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">[CLS]</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>∈</mo><mi>S</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x(S)=(\texttt{[CLS]},\,q,\,\{p_{i}\}_{i\in S}).</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">We apply a single multi-head self-attention layer followed by a lightweight feed-forward block. The final set score is obtained from the <span id="A1.SS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[CLS]</span> output:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex9" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex9.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s(q,S)=w^{\top}h_{\texttt{[CLS]}}(S)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><msup><mi>w</mi><mo>⊤</mo></msup><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">[CLS]</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s(q,S)=w^{\top}h_{\texttt{[CLS]}}(S),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS2.p1.3" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h_{\texttt{[CLS]}}(S)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_monospace">[CLS]</mtext></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h_{\texttt{[CLS]}}(S)</annotation></semantics></math> is the <span id="A1.SS2.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">[CLS]</span> representation after the single attention layer (and optional FFN).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.3 </span>Example of Set Quality Ordering</h3>

<div id="A1.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We illustrate the set quality ordering used in our margin-based objective.
Suppose the gold evidence set for a query is</p>
<table id="A1.Ex10" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex10.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{q}=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+}\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{q}=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.2" class="ltx_p">For a candidate set <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math>, we compute recall and precision with respect to <math id="A1.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{G}_{q}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{G}_{q}</annotation></semantics></math>:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex11" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex11.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Recall}(S)=\frac{|S\cap\mathcal{G}_{q}|}{|\mathcal{G}_{q}|},\qquad\mathrm{Precision}(S)=\frac{|S\cap\mathcal{G}_{q}|}{|S|}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mrow><mrow><mi>Recall</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="2.167em">,</mo><mrow><mrow><mi>Precision</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>∩</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒢</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Recall}(S)=\frac{|S\cap\mathcal{G}_{q}|}{|\mathcal{G}_{q}|},\qquad\mathrm{Precision}(S)=\frac{|S\cap\mathcal{G}_{q}|}{|S|}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS3.p1.3" class="ltx_p">We then rank candidate sets lexicographically by recall first and precision second.
That is, a set with higher recall is preferred; if two sets have the same recall, the one with higher precision is preferred.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">For example, consider the following candidate sets:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex12" class="ltx_equationgroup ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody id="A1.Ex12X"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12X.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle S_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle S_{1}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12X.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+}\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A1.Ex12Xa"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12Xa.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle S_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle S_{2}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12Xa.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+},d^{-}\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+},d^{-}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A1.Ex12Xb"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12Xb.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle S_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle S_{3}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12Xb.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\{d_{1}^{+}\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\{d_{1}^{+}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A1.Ex12Xc"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12Xc.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle S_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle S_{4}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12Xc.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\{d_{1}^{+},d^{-}\}," display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\{d_{1}^{+},d^{-}\},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
<tbody id="A1.Ex12Xd"><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12Xd.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle S_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle S_{5}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_eqn_cell"><math id="A1.Ex12Xd.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\displaystyle=\{d^{-}\}." display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\displaystyle=\{d^{-}\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">Here, <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{1}</annotation></semantics></math> is the complete gold set, <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{2}</annotation></semantics></math> is an addition perturbation, <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{3}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{3}</annotation></semantics></math> is an elimination perturbation, <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{4}</annotation></semantics></math> is an interchange-like corrupted set, and <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> is a fully negative set.
Their recall and precision values are:</p>
<table id="A1.Ex13" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex13.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}\text{Set}&amp;\mathrm{Recall}&amp;\mathrm{Precision}\\
\hline\cr S_{1}=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+}\}&amp;1.0&amp;1.0\\
S_{2}=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+},d^{-}\}&amp;1.0&amp;2/3\\
S_{3}=\{d_{1}^{+}\}&amp;1/2&amp;1.0\\
S_{4}=\{d_{1}^{+},d^{-}\}&amp;1/2&amp;1/2\\
S_{5}=\{d^{-}\}&amp;0.0&amp;0.0\\
\end{array}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mtable columnspacing="5pt" displaystyle="true" rowspacing="0pt"><mtr><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mtext>Set</mtext></mtd><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mi>Recall</mi></mtd><mtd><mi>Precision</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_border_t"></mtd><mtd class="ltx_border_t"></mtd><mtd class="ltx_border_t"></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mn>1.0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>1.0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mn>1.0</mn></mtd><mtd><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mn>1.0</mn></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mtd><mtd><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msup><mi>d</mi><mo>−</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow></mtd><mtd class="ltx_border_r"><mn>0.0</mn></mtd><mtd><mn>0.0</mn></mtd></mtr></mtable><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}\text{Set}&amp;\mathrm{Recall}&amp;\mathrm{Precision}\\
\hline\cr S_{1}=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+}\}&amp;1.0&amp;1.0\\
S_{2}=\{d_{1}^{+},d_{2}^{+},d^{-}\}&amp;1.0&amp;2/3\\
S_{3}=\{d_{1}^{+}\}&amp;1/2&amp;1.0\\
S_{4}=\{d_{1}^{+},d^{-}\}&amp;1/2&amp;1/2\\
S_{5}=\{d^{-}\}&amp;0.0&amp;0.0\\
\end{array}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.3" class="ltx_p">Therefore, the induced ordering is</p>
<table id="A1.Ex14" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex14.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S_{1}\succ S_{2}\succ S_{3}\succ S_{4}\succ S_{5}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>≻</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>≻</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>3</mn></msub><mo>≻</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>4</mn></msub><mo>≻</mo><msub><mi>S</mi><mn>5</mn></msub></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S_{1}\succ S_{2}\succ S_{3}\succ S_{4}\succ S_{5}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS3.p2.4" class="ltx_p">This ordering captures the intuition that covering all required evidence is most important, but among sets with the same coverage, more compact and less noisy sets should be preferred.
The margin loss in Eq. (<a href="#S3.E1" title="In Training objective. ‣ 3.1 Set-level Compatibility Learning ‣ 3 Set-Level Query–Set Scoring ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) is then applied to ordered pairs <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(H,L)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(H,L)</annotation></semantics></math> where <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math> appears above <math id="A1.SS3.p2.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="L" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>L</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">L</annotation></semantics></math> under this ordering.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">A.4 </span>Beam-Search Set Retrieval</h3>

<div id="A1.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our objective is to approximately solve</p>
<table id="A1.Ex15" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex15.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S^{\star}=\arg\max_{S\subseteq[n],\,S\neq\varnothing}s(q,S)," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mo>⋆</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>arg</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><munder><mi>max</mi><mrow><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⊆</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow></mrow><mo rspace="0.337em">,</mo><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>≠</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">∅</mi></mrow></mrow></munder><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S^{\star}=\arg\max_{S\subseteq[n],\,S\neq\varnothing}s(q,S),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS4.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of candidate passages.
Since there are <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2^{n}-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>n</mi></msup><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2^{n}-1</annotation></semantics></math> non-empty subsets, exhaustive enumeration is infeasible except for very small <math id="A1.SS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>n</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n</annotation></semantics></math>.
We therefore employ a <em id="A1.SS4.p1.2.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">depth-limited beam search</em> with batched set scoring.</p>
</div>
<div id="A1.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In practice, we restrict the maximum size of candidate sets during inference to a predefined limit <math id="A1.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>.
This constraint reflects the observation that multi-hop question answering typically requires only a small number of supporting passages, and it prevents unnecessary expansion into overly large and noisy sets.</p>
</div>
<section id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Initialization and expansion.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first score all singleton sets and retain the top-<math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> as the initial beam.
At each iteration, every beam subset <math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>S</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S</annotation></semantics></math> is expanded by adding new passages from the remaining pool.
The expansion proceeds only if <math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|S|&lt;T_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|S|&lt;T_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, ensuring that the beam search explores sets up to a bounded size.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Expansion.</h4>

<div id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For step <math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="t=2,3,\dots,T_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">t=2,3,\dots,T_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, we expand each beam subset by adding new elements from the remaining pool.
Let <math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the maximum number of newly added passages per expansion step (in our standard setting, <math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="a_{\max}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">a_{\max}=1</annotation></semantics></math>).
For each <math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S\in\mathcal{B}_{t-1}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>∈</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S\in\mathcal{B}_{t-1}</annotation></semantics></math> with <math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|S|&lt;T_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&lt;</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>max</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|S|&lt;T_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, we generate candidate sets</p>
<table id="A1.Ex16" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A1.Ex16.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="\mathcal{N}(S)=\left\{S\cup A:A\subseteq[n]\setminus S,\ 1\leq|A|\leq a_{\max}\right\}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒩</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>=</mo><mrow><mo>{</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>∪</mo><mi>A</mi><mo lspace="0.278em" rspace="0.278em">:</mo><mi>A</mi><mo>⊆</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><mo>∖</mo><mi>S</mi><mo>,</mo><mn> 1</mn><mo rspace="0em">≤</mo><mo fence="false" rspace="0.167em" stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>A</mi><mo fence="false" stretchy="false">|</mo><mo lspace="0.167em">≤</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>}</mo></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{N}(S)=\left\{S\cup A:A\subseteq[n]\setminus S,\ 1\leq|A|\leq a_{\max}\right\}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">All generated candidates are scored in batch, deduplicated, and the top-<math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>B</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B</annotation></semantics></math> subsets are retained as the next beam <math id="A1.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}_{t}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}_{t}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Robustness Analysis of Sequential Set Scoring</h2>

<figure id="A2.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2607.05712v1/beamce_robustness_intro_two_figures.svg" id="A2.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/204;" width="476" height="204"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>
Controlled analysis of sequential retrieval robustness on MuSiQue.
We compare a sequential scorer trained with local BCE supervision against the same architecture fine-tuned with our set-level compatibility objective.
Left: prefixes consist only of distractor passages.
Right: prefixes contain partial gold evidence and additional distractors, leaving one unseen gold passage as the retrieval target.
Set-level compatibility learning yields more stable retrieval precision as prefixes become longer and noisier.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We conduct a controlled analysis to examine whether sequential retrieval models can robustly evaluate query–set interactions under variable-length and noisy retrieval chains.
We compare a sequential list-level scorer trained with pointwise BCE supervision, following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al. (2024)</a></cite>, against the same architecture fine-tuned only with our set-level compatibility learning objective.
Thus, the two models differ only in their training objective, not in architecture or inference procedure.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A2.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Appendix B Robustness Analysis of Sequential Set Scoring ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> shows results on MuSiQue under two controlled prefix settings.
In the distractor-only setting, the retrieved prefix consists entirely of irrelevant passages.
In the partially-gold setting, for an <math id="A2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>H</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H</annotation></semantics></math>-hop question, the prefix contains only gold passages when <math id="A2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T&lt;H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T&lt;H</annotation></semantics></math>; once <math id="A2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T\geq H" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>≥</mo><mi>H</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T\geq H</annotation></semantics></math>, we include <math id="A2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H-1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H-1</annotation></semantics></math> gold passages and fill the remaining positions with distractors, leaving exactly one unseen gold passage as the retrieval target.
Retrieval precision measures the success rate of retrieving this target gold passage given a prefix of length <math id="A2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>T</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The scorer trained with local BCE supervision degrades sharply as the prefix becomes longer or noisier.
This suggests that local next-passage supervision does not sufficiently encourage the model to evaluate the compatibility of the full query–prefix context, especially when retrieval errors accumulate.
By contrast, the same model fine-tuned with our set-level compatibility objective remains substantially more stable across both settings.
This supports our claim that set-level supervision improves robustness to variable-length and partially corrupted evidence contexts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Additional Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Results</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In § <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Trade-off ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>, we report the effectiveness–efficiency trade-off on HotpotQA using retrieval <math id="A3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is most strongly correlated with downstream QA EM in our analysis.
Here, we provide additional results on all three datasets to show that the observed trade-off is not specific to HotpotQA.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.F5" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2607.05712v1/contriever_tradeoff_comprehensive_f5.svg" id="A3.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/107;" width="405" height="107"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>
Retrieval <math id="A3.F5.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> versus latency across HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue using Contriever as the first-stage retriever.
Each curve varies the number of first-stage candidate passages with <math id="A3.F5.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\in\{5,10,\dots,50\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\in\{5,10,\dots,50\}</annotation></semantics></math>, and each point corresponds to one value of <math id="A3.F5.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>, left-to-right order.
The <math id="A3.F5.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="x" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>x</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>-axis reports per-query latency on a logarithmic scale; for all methods except Bi, we exclude the first-stage bi-encoder retrieval time.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#A3.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Additional Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Results ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> extends the analysis in Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Trade-off ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> to all three datasets.
Across datasets, document-level CE provides a low-latency reranking baseline, while applying set-level cross-encoder scoring throughout beam search is substantially more expensive.
<span id="A3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> remains lightweight because it performs late interaction over precomputed and KV-cached embeddings, allowing it to explore larger candidate pools with limited additional cost.
The combined <span id="A3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A3.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> pipeline improves the trade-off by separating the roles of exploration and reranking: <span id="A3.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> first searches over candidate evidence sets, and <span id="A3.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> is then applied only to a reduced pool of candidate sets.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This distinction is important because beam-search <span id="A3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> invokes the cross-encoder scorer repeatedly over intermediate candidate sets, whereas <span id="A3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> pays the cross-encoder cost only after lightweight set exploration.
In our latency measurements, beam-search <span id="A3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> at <math id="A3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=20</annotation></semantics></math> requires 0.555 seconds per query, while <span id="A3.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A3.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> at <math id="A3.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=50</annotation></semantics></math> requires only 0.116 seconds per query.
Thus, the proposed retrieve-and-rerank design can use a larger first-stage candidate pool while avoiding cross-encoder scoring over the full beam-search space.</p>
</div>
<section id="A3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.1 </span>Correlation between Retrieval Metrics and QA EM</h3>

<div id="A3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Section <a href="#S4.SS4" title="4.4 Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Trade-off ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.4</span></a>, we use retrieval <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> as the primary metric for the effectiveness–efficiency analysis.
Here, we provide the full correlation results that motivate this choice.
We compute retrieval precision, recall, and <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\beta}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>β</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\beta}</annotation></semantics></math> scores across all methods, datasets, and first-stage retrievers used in our end-to-end QA experiments, and measure their Pearson correlation with QA EM:</p>
<table id="A3.Ex17" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A3.Ex17.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{\beta}=\frac{(1+\beta^{2})\cdot\mathrm{Precision}\cdot\mathrm{Recall}}{\beta^{2}\cdot\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mi>β</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>Precision</mi><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>Recall</mi></mrow><mrow><mrow><msup><mi>β</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mi>Precision</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo><mi>Recall</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{\beta}=\frac{(1+\beta^{2})\cdot\mathrm{Precision}\cdot\mathrm{Recall}}{\beta^{2}\cdot\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A3.SS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">Precision corresponds to <math id="A3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, while recall corresponds to the large-<math id="A3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> limit.</p>

Precision corresponds to <math id="A3.T4.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{0}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{0}</annotation></semantics></math>, while recall corresponds to the large-<math id="A3.T4.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math> limit.

</table>
</figure>
<div id="A3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">As shown in Table <a href="#A3.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ C.1 Correlation between Retrieval Metrics and QA EM ‣ Appendix C Additional Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Results ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, precision alone correlates weakly with QA EM, while recall is substantially more predictive.
The correlation peaks at <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> and slightly decreases for larger <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\beta" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>β</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\beta</annotation></semantics></math>.
This suggests that downstream QA is strongly coverage-sensitive, but still benefits from penalizing overly noisy retrieved contexts.
We therefore use <math id="A3.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> as a finite recall-oriented metric in the main effectiveness–efficiency analysis.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.2 </span>Precision–recall behavior.</h3>

<div id="A3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Because <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> is a recall-oriented metric, it is also useful to inspect precision and recall separately.
Precision measures the fraction of selected passages that are gold evidence, while recall measures the fraction of gold evidence passages covered by the selected set.
In multi-hop QA, recall is often more predictive of downstream answerability because missing a required evidence passage prevents the reader from deriving the answer.
However, recall alone ignores the cost of adding distractors, so we use <math id="A3.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="F_{5}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>5</mn></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">F_{5}</annotation></semantics></math> as a finite recall-oriented metric that still penalizes unnecessarily noisy contexts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">C.3 </span>Analysis of Selected Evidence Set Size</h3>

<div id="A3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond retrieval accuracy and latency, set-level methods differ from passage-level rerankers in the number of passages they return.
A standard passage-level cross-encoder produces a ranked list of individual passages, and in our evaluation we provide a fixed top-5 list to the answer generator.
In contrast, set-level methods directly score candidate passage sets, so the final output can contain a variable number of passages depending on the query and candidate pool.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ C.3 Analysis of Selected Evidence Set Size ‣ Appendix C Additional Retrieval Effectiveness–Efficiency Results ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> reports the average number of selected passages on 2WikiMultiHopQA for different first-stage candidate sizes <math id="A3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>.
The CE baseline always returns five passages, reflecting its fixed top-5 evaluation protocol.
Set-level methods, however, produce variable-size evidence sets.
This highlights a qualitative difference between passage-level reranking and set-level retrieval: the latter selects an evidence set rather than a fixed-length ranked list.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A3.T5" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 5: </span>
Average number of passages selected on 2WikiMultiHopQA.
Unlike CE, which returns a fixed top-5 list, set-level methods select variable-size evidence sets.
The average number of gold supporting passages is 2.5.

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Hop-wise End-to-End QA Performance</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix D Hop-wise End-to-End QA Performance ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> reports the full hop-wise downstream QA results corresponding to the macro-average results in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
We report EM and F1 for each available hop category.
HotpotQA contains only 2-hop questions, whereas 2WikiMultihopQA and MuSiQue include questions with different reasoning depths.
The macro-average is computed by averaging performance across the available hop categories for each dataset.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">These results provide a more fine-grained view of the behavior of different retrieval methods.
Overall, the trends are consistent with the main results in Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
Set-level compatibility learning often improves over locally supervised sequential retrieval, as shown by the comparison between <span id="A4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ListCE</span> and <span id="A4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>.
In addition, <span id="A4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> is particularly effective in several higher-hop settings, suggesting that explicit query–set scoring can be useful when evidence must be selected as a coherent group rather than as independently relevant passages.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 6: </span>
Hop-wise downstream QA performance with two first-stage retrievers.
We report EM / F1 (%) for each hop category and the macro-average across available hops.

<section id="A4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">D.1 </span>Efficiency of Combined Retrieval Pipelines</h3>

<div id="A4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide additional efficiency measurements for the retrieval and reranking pipelines used in our experiments.
The goal of this analysis is to quantify the computational overhead introduced by combining document-level and set-level outputs, as used in the CE-augmentation setting in § <a href="#S4.SS3" title="4.3 Complementarity of Document-Level and Set-Level Scoring ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We report two metrics.
First, we measure inference latency in seconds per query while varying the number of first-stage candidate passages <math id="A4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math>.
Second, we measure peak GPU memory usage in GB.
The memory measurement captures the maximum allocated memory during actual inference, rather than the memory required only to load the model.
All measurements are conducted under the same inference configuration used in our main experiments.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ D.1 Efficiency of Combined Retrieval Pipelines ‣ Appendix D Hop-wise End-to-End QA Performance ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> reports latency for <math id="A4.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K\in\{5,10,\ldots,50\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K\in\{5,10,\ldots,50\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Table <a href="#A4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ D.1 Efficiency of Combined Retrieval Pipelines ‣ Appendix D Hop-wise End-to-End QA Performance ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> reports peak memory usage at <math id="A4.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=20" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>20</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=20</annotation></semantics></math>.
The results show that combining document-level and set-level outputs introduces only moderate additional overhead.
This is because the combined pipelines reuse the document-level output and augment it with a compact set-level output, rather than requiring exhaustive scoring over all possible passage combinations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A4.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, these measurements support the practical feasibility of combining document-level and set-level evidence.
The combined pipelines improve downstream QA performance while keeping inference latency and peak memory usage within a modest range.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A4.T7" class="ltx_table">

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Additional Experiments</h2>

<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Comparison with LLM-based Set Retrieval</h3>

<div id="A5.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our methods with an LLM-based set selection baseline inspired by SETR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, a representative set-level retrieval method.
The original SETR framework fine-tunes a Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model for set retrieval.
We approximate this SETR-style paradigm (especially, SETR-CoT&amp;IRI in  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lee et al., 2025</a>)</cite>) using GPT-4o-mini, the same model used for answer generation in our QA evaluation, as a LLM set selection.
Except for replacing the fine-tuned SETR model with this frozen LLM selector, we keep the evaluation pipeline, candidate passages, prompting format consistent with the original SETR framework.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ E.1 Comparison with LLM-based Set Retrieval ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a> reports downstream QA performance on HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue.
Our methods achieve performance that is competitive with SETR across all datasets.
On HotpotQA, <span id="A5.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A5.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> outperforms SETR in both EM and F1.
On 2WikiMultihopQA, SETR achieves slightly higher EM, while <span id="A5.SS1.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A5.SS1.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> achieves higher F1.
On MuSiQue, SETR achieves the highest EM, while <span id="A5.SS1.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> achieves the highest F1.
Overall, these results suggest that explicit set-level compatibility learning can provide comparable set-selection quality to LLM-based set retrieval.</p>
</div>
