<div id="A5.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">We also compare the computational cost of SETR and our set-level methods.
Table <a href="#A5.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ E.1 Comparison with LLM-based Set Retrieval ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> reports peak memory usage and inference latency.
Because SETR performs LLM-based set selection, it requires substantially higher memory and latency than our neural set scorers.
In contrast, <span id="A5.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> and <span id="A5.SS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A5.SS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> achieve comparable set-selection quality with much lower computational cost.
This supports the practical motivation of our framework: set-level retrieval can be performed effectively without relying on expensive LLM-based selection.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T10" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 10: </span>
Efficiency comparison with SETR.
Memory denotes GPU memory usage after loading the model, before running inference.
Latency is measured in seconds per query during inference.
</figcaption>

<td id="A5.T10.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:0.25pt;padding-bottom:0.25pt;"><span id="A5.T10.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Memory (GB)</span></td>

</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Candidate Quality and Standalone Performance of <span id="A5.SS2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span></h3>

<div id="A5.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> is designed to function as a lightweight set-level explorer.
Its role is analogous to a first-stage retriever in the set space: it efficiently searches over a combinatorial space of candidate passage sets and returns a small pool of promising sets for subsequent reranking.
Therefore, evaluating only the top-ranked set can underestimate its usefulness in the full retrieve-and-rerank pipeline.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To better characterize this behavior, we evaluate Max-F1@<math id="A5.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Given the top-<math id="A5.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> candidate sets produced by <span id="A5.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>, Max-F1@<math id="A5.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> is defined as the maximum retrieval F1 among those candidate sets.
This metric measures whether <span id="A5.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> can place high-quality evidence sets within a small candidate pool, even when its top-1 prediction is not optimal.
We vary two parameters:
<math id="A5.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, the number of first-stage candidate passages retrieved by the bi-encoder, and
<math id="A5.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, the number of candidate sets produced by <span id="A5.SS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> and passed to the reranker.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ E.2 Candidate Quality and Standalone Performance of ParaSet ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> reports Max-F1@<math id="A5.SS2.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> on MuSiQue.
For a fixed <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{b}</annotation></semantics></math>, Max-F1 consistently improves as <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> increases.
This shows that <span id="A5.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> often retrieves useful candidate sets within its top-<math id="A5.SS2.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> outputs, supporting its role as a set-level explorer.
At the same time, for a fixed <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math>, performance can decrease as <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> increases.
This is expected because increasing <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> expands the set search space combinatorially, making it more difficult for a lightweight model to identify the best set at top-1 or within a very small candidate budget.
In practice, larger candidate pools may require larger <math id="A5.SS2.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> so that the downstream reranker receives sufficient candidate coverage.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T11" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 11: </span>
Max-F1@<math id="A5.T11.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> of <span id="A5.T11.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> on MuSiQue.
<math id="A5.T11.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{b}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{b}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of first-stage candidate passages retrieved by the bi-encoder, and <math id="A5.T11.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the number of top candidate sets produced by <span id="A5.T11.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>.
</figcaption>
<table id="A5.T11.6" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">

<div id="A5.SS2.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p4.1" class="ltx_p">These results clarify the role of <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> in our framework.
<span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> is not optimized to be the most accurate final scorer at top-1.
Instead, its primary purpose is to efficiently explore the set space and provide a compact candidate pool for a more expressive reranker such as <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span>.
The consistent improvement from <math id="A5.SS2.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}=1</annotation></semantics></math> to larger <math id="A5.SS2.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k_{p}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k_{p}</annotation></semantics></math> values indicates that <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> can provide useful candidate coverage, which is precisely the desired behavior in the <span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A5.SS2.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> pipeline.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS2.p5.1" class="ltx_p">For completeness, we also report the standalone QA performance of <span id="A5.SS2.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> in Table <a href="#A5.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ E.2 Candidate Quality and Standalone Performance of ParaSet ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>.
As expected, <span id="A5.SS2.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> alone is not always the strongest final scorer, especially on datasets where the best evidence set is difficult to identify from a large combinatorial candidate space.
This behavior is consistent with its intended role as a lightweight set-level explorer rather than a high-capacity reranker.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T12" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 12: </span>

</figcaption>

</span></div>

</section>
<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Comparison with Agentic Retrieval Pipelines</h3>

<div id="A5.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We compare our retrieve-at-once setting with IRCoT-style agentic retrieval pipelines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2023</a>)</cite>.
Agentic pipelines iteratively generate intermediate queries, retrieve new passages, and perform intermediate reasoning, which can improve exploration but requires multiple LLM calls and repeated retrieval operations.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate agentic variants equipped with a bi-encoder retriever and with a bi-encoder followed by CE reranking.
For our methods, retrieval is performed once and the selected passage set is directly provided to the answer-generation LLM.
Table <a href="#A5.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ E.3 Comparison with Agentic Retrieval Pipelines ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a> reports the results on MuSiQue.
Our set-level methods are competitive with the agentic baselines while avoiding iterative LLM-driven retrieval.
In particular, the CE-augmented <span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A5.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> variant achieves the best macro EM and performs especially well on 4-hop questions, suggesting that a one-shot combination of document-level and set-level evidence can recover useful multi-hop contexts without iterative retrieval.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ E.3 Comparison with Agentic Retrieval Pipelines ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> further compares inference latency.
The multi-step agentic pipelines require substantially more time per query because they repeatedly invoke the LLM and retrieval modules across reasoning steps.
In contrast, our single-step set-level methods perform retrieval only once.
As a result, <span id="A5.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> is about <math id="A5.SS3.p3.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="15.0\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>15.0</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">15.0\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster than the multi-step CE pipeline, <span id="A5.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A5.SS3.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> is about <math id="A5.SS3.p3.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="74.5\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>74.5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">74.5\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster, and <span id="A5.SS3.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>+<span id="A5.SS3.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> (<math id="A5.SS3.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\cup" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>∪</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cup</annotation></semantics></math> CE) remains about <math id="A5.SS3.p3.m4" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="44.1\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>44.1</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">44.1\times</annotation></semantics></math> faster while achieving strong downstream performance.
These results highlight the practical advantage of retrieve-at-once set-level scoring over iterative agentic retrieval.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T13" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 13: </span>
Comparison between multi-step (agentic) and single-step retrieval settings on the MuSiQue dataset.
We report QA EM for each hop category and the macro average.
</figcaption>
<div id="A5.T13.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:280.8pt;height:218.3pt;vertical-align:-107.0pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-24.8pt,19.3pt) scale(0.8,0.8) ;">
<table id="A5.T13.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A5.T13.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T13.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:0.75pt;padding-bottom:0.75pt;"><span id="A5.T13.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hop</span></td>
<td id="A5.T13.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-top:0.75pt;padding-bottom:0.75pt;"><span id="A5.T13.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Retrieval Setting</span></td>

<section id="A5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.4 </span>Beam Width Analysis</h3>

<div id="A5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We analyze the effect of beam width during <span id="A5.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> inference.
A larger beam allows the model to explore more candidate sets, but also increases inference cost.
Table <a href="#A5.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ E.4 Beam Width Analysis ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> reports retrieval F1 and relative inference speed on MuSiQue.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Increasing the beam width from 1 to 2 improves retrieval F1, suggesting that limited branching is useful for set exploration.
However, further increasing the beam width yields little additional gain while substantially reducing speed.
We therefore use a small beam width in the main experiments.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T15" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 15: </span>
Retrieval F1 and relative inference speed of <span id="A5.T15.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> on MuSiQue with different beam widths.
Inference speed is normalized by the beam width of 1.
</figcaption>

</figure>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.5 </span>Effect of Adjacent-Ranking Weight</h3>

<div id="A5.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This section provides a detailed analysis of how the weight of the fine-grained adjacent-ranking term (<math id="A5.SS5.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> in Eq. <a href="#S3.E1" title="In Training objective. ‣ 3.1 Set-level Compatibility Learning ‣ 3 Set-Level Query–Set Scoring ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>) influences the <em id="A5.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">set size bias</em> of <span id="A5.SS5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Recall that the training objective consists of a coarse ranking constraint that enforces the gold set to be ranked above all candidates, together with an adjacent-ranking term:</p>
<table id="A5.Ex18" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex18.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{final}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{pos-all}}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{adj}}." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>final</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>pos-all</mtext></msub><mo>+</mo><mrow><mi>λ</mi><mo lspace="0.170em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>adj</mtext></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo lspace="0em">.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{final}}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{pos-all}}+\lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{adj}}.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS5.p2.2" class="ltx_p">The adjacent-ranking loss <math id="A5.SS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{L}_{\text{adj}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℒ</mi><mtext>adj</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{L}_{\text{adj}}</annotation></semantics></math> provides finer-grained supervision by contrasting candidate sets that differ only subtly in quality under a predefined set-quality ordering (recall-first and precision-second in our experiments).
Increasing <math id="A5.SS5.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> therefore strengthens the pressure to separate nearby candidate sets generated through structured perturbations such as <span id="A5.SS5.p2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">addition</span>, <span id="A5.SS5.p2.2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">elimination</span>, and <span id="A5.SS5.p2.2.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">interchange</span>, as well as negatives induced implicitly by in-batch sampling.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For each dataset, we train <span id="A5.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> with different values of <math id="A5.SS5.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> while keeping all other hyperparameters fixed.
At inference time, we retrieve the top-20 documents using a bi-encoder and apply <span id="A5.SS5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> to rank candidate passage sets constructed from this fixed pool.
To quantify how the strength of adjacent-ranking supervision affects retrieval behavior, we measure the <em id="A5.SS5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">average size of the top-ranked set</em> predicted by <span id="A5.SS5.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span>.
Here, the top-ranked set refers to the single highest-scoring candidate set under <math id="A5.SS5.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="S(q,\cdot)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>q</mi><mo rspace="0em">,</mo><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">⋅</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">S(q,\cdot)</annotation></semantics></math> among all sets considered during inference.
This metric captures whether training encourages the model to favor more <em id="A5.SS5.p3.1.5" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">parsimonious</em> sets with fewer documents, or more <em id="A5.SS5.p3.1.6" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">inclusive</em> sets that incorporate additional, potentially redundant evidence.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T16" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 16: </span>
Dataset statistics for the multi-hop QA benchmarks used in our experiments.
We report the standard train/dev/test split sizes.
</figcaption>
<table id="A5.T16.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A5.T16.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T16.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.25pt 5.0pt;"><span id="A5.T16.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dataset</span></td>
<td id="A5.T16.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.25pt 5.0pt;"><span id="A5.T16.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Train</span></td>
<td id="A5.T16.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.25pt 5.0pt;"><span id="A5.T16.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Dev</span></td>
<td id="A5.T16.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.25pt 5.0pt;"><span id="A5.T16.2.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Test</span></td>
<td id="A5.T16.2.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.25pt 5.0pt;"><span id="A5.T16.2.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hop Categories</span></td></tr>

<td id="A5.T18.4.4.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="padding:0.5pt 8.0pt;">3.320</td></tr>
</table>
</figure>
<div id="A5.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T18" title="Table 18 ‣ E.5 Effect of Adjacent-Ranking Weight ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a> reports the average size of the top-ranked predicted set across three datasets.
The effect of <math id="A5.SS5.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> is highly dataset-dependent.
On <span id="A5.SS5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2WikiMultihopQA</span>, increasing <math id="A5.SS5.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> leads to a consistent decrease in the predicted set size, from 4.08 to 3.35.
Given that the average number of gold supporting documents in this dataset is approximately 2.4, this trend suggests that stronger adjacent-ranking supervision helps prune non-essential documents while preserving coverage of relevant evidence.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS5.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS5.p5.1" class="ltx_p">In contrast, <span id="A5.SS5.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">HotpotQA</span> exhibits the opposite behavior: as <math id="A5.SS5.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> increases, the predicted set size grows sharply and saturates near the candidate limit.
This suggests that, under HotpotQA’s evidence distribution, overweighting adjacent-ranking constraints can bias the model toward overly inclusive sets.
Finally, <span id="A5.SS5.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MuSiQue</span> also shows an increasing trend in set size with larger <math id="A5.SS5.p5.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math>, although the effect is more moderate.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS5.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.SS5.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, these results highlight <math id="A5.SS5.p6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\lambda" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>λ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\lambda</annotation></semantics></math> as a critical hyperparameter that governs the trade-off between coverage and parsimony in set-level retrieval.
Importantly, its optimal value is not universal but depends on dataset-specific properties such as the typical number of supporting documents and the prevalence of plausible yet irrelevant distractors.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Artifacts, Licenses, and Intended Use</h2>

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use publicly available benchmarks and pretrained models for research purposes.
The datasets used in our experiments are HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, and MuSiQue.
The pretrained retrieval and reranking models include Contriever, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, <span id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ms-marco-electra-base</span>, and <span id="A6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">deberta-v3-base</span>.
We cite the original creators of these artifacts in the main text and bibliography.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our use of these artifacts is limited to academic research on retrieval and multi-hop question answering.
We do not redistribute the original datasets or pretrained model weights.
Users should consult the original licenses and terms of use for each dataset and model before redistribution or deployment.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The datasets used in this work are existing public QA benchmarks.
We do not collect new human-subject data, recruit annotators, or create additional personally identifying information.
Because the datasets may contain text derived from public web or Wikipedia-like sources, we do not claim that they are free of all sensitive or offensive content.
However, our work does not attempt to identify individuals, infer private attributes, or deanonymize any data.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix G </span>Dataset Statistics and Computational Budget</h2>

<section id="A7.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.1 </span>Dataset Statistics</h3>

<div id="A7.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ E.5 Effect of Adjacent-Ranking Weight ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> reports the standard train/dev/test split sizes of the multi-hop QA benchmarks used in our experiments.
We use HotpotQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2018</a>)</cite>, 2WikiMultihopQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ho et al., 2020</a>)</cite>, and MuSiQue <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Trivedi et al., 2022</a>)</cite>.
For MuSiQue, we report the statistics of MuSiQue-Ans, which is the answerable split commonly used for multi-hop QA evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A7.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">G.2 </span>Model Size and Computational Budget</h3>

<div id="A7.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#A5.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ E.5 Effect of Adjacent-Ranking Weight ‣ Appendix E Additional Experiments ‣ Retrieving a Set, Not Independent Passages: Set-Level Compatibility Learning for Efficient Set Exploration" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> reports the parameter counts of the main trainable retrieval models used in our experiments.
<span id="A7.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ListCE</span> and <span id="A7.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">SetCE</span> share the same cross-encoder backbone and differ only in the training objective.
<span id="A7.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> is substantially smaller because it operates over precomputed bi-encoder embeddings with a lightweight late-interaction layer.
The parameter count of <span id="A7.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">ParaSet</span> depends on the embedding dimensionality of the first-stage retriever, resulting in different sizes for Contriever and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B.</p>
</div>
<div id="A7.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All latency measurements reported in the main text and appendix are measured on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU with 24GB memory.
We report latency in seconds per query under the inference configurations used in the experiments.
For all methods except the first-stage bi-encoder baseline, the reported latency excludes the shared first-stage retrieval time and measures the additional retrieval/reranking cost.
We do not train any foundation-scale language model or embedding model from scratch; our computational budget is limited to training lightweight set scorers and fine-tuning reranking models on top of publicly available pretrained checkpoints.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</article>
</div>
